intro: Stock’s Victor record explicitly credits the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and grand organ; the recording ledger names organist Walter P. Zimmerman. Its 4:25 transfer is almost the same length as Elgar’s, leaving local phrasing rather than total duration as the useful comparison.
question: Can two nearly equal total durations conceal different decisions about phrase length and orchestral weight?

cues.title: Organ is documented
cues.text: The label says “Chicago Symphony Orchestra and Grand Organ”. DAHR identifies Walter P. Zimmerman as organist; listen for the sustained foundation, but do not assume every low sound belongs to the organ rather than the orchestral basses.
cues.evidence: Victrola 6648-B label and DAHR matrix CVE-37282, https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800011535. This concerns the credited ensemble; the analysis does not isolate an organ entrance.

cues.title: A recorded orchestral complement
cues.text: Victor’s ledger lists twelve first violins, thirteen seconds, eleven violas, eight cellos and eight basses for the session. Those numbers document the players assembled, not their relative prominence in the transfer.
cues.evidence: DAHR CVE-37282 Additional Information reproduces the Victor ledger instrumentation. DAHR cautions that wind doubling makes exact instrumentation uncertain; the listed string counts are reported directly.

cues.title: Withdrawal before the line
cues.text: The quieter passage follows a pronounced drop in recorded level. Compare the long melody’s line with the short gestures of the march rather than treating quieter playing as a new tempo measurement.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-stock-1926.txt: strongest boundary at 1:14; level changes from −7.1 dB at 1:05 to −18.2 at 1:15. Formal identification is approximate and follows the work’s march/trio contrast.

cues.title: Session and issue differ
cues.text: DAHR dates the issued master to 22 December 1926. The trade announcement lists Victor 6648 for release on 1 July 1927; confusing those dates moves the performance into the wrong year.
cues.evidence: DAHR CVE-37282: take 3, 22 December 1926, Orchestra Hall, Chicago. The Talking Machine World, June 1927, p. 157, Victor list for 1 July, announces 6648. Internet Archive’s 1926 date is not independent publication evidence.

cues.title: Equal length, different phrasing
cues.text: This complete transfer lasts about 4:25, against about 4:24 for Elgar. Such close totals need not make corresponding phrases equally long: compare the returning march before judging either conductor by a single duration.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-stock-1926.txt gives 265.5 seconds; the Elgar report gives 264.1. The comparison map uses 5–258 seconds of both files and measures local correspondences rather than inferring them from total length.

cues.title: The broad tune returns
cues.text: In the later broad melody, compare the sustained bass and the upper line. The organ credit makes the lower foundation a particular question for this recording, not proof that any single layer can be separated by ear.
cues.evidence: DAHR establishes orchestra and organ. cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-stock-1926.txt places a boundary at 3:10 and a high-level span thereafter; it cannot separate organ, strings and brass.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Keeping the crest alive
cues.text: The strongest sustained level region lies late in the performance, then diminishes towards the close. Follow how the broad line remains connected across that crest before the short ending releases it.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-stock-1926.txt: loudest five-second windows cluster at 3:30–3:50; level is −3.5 dB at 3:50, −6.4 at 4:05 and −9.6 at 4:10. The large fall by 4:20 includes the end of the side.

facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
